pr_title: Restrict the index authorization checks in PIT search
pr_body:
Search requests executed against a PIT do not have to set the target indices explicitly. Instead the list of targeted index is extracted from the PIT id directly. When executed against the search rest layer, the indices of the PIT are copied in the search request in order to fullfill the authorization check when security is enabled. However, this crucial copy operation is omitted when the search request is internally executed from a node within the cluster. Consequently, the authorization check ends up evaluating the request against all indices accessible to the user. To address this performance issue, the proposed change ensures this copy occurs explicitly within the security layer. This modification restricts the authorization check to indices that are part of the PIT, mitigating the performance bug. It is essential to note that even in the presence of this bug, the request does not route to all indices; only those present in the PIT are queried. Furthermore, this issue is not a security vulnerability, as the authorization check continues to limit the list of accessible indices to those permitted for the user.

Closes #99684
pr_comments: The PR is ready for another round of review @javanna . @przemekwitek can you take a look at the changes I made to the transform indexer?
@jimczi do you think this would be safe to backport?

@javanna I think it's relatively safe but the impact on performance should be minimal so I am not sure if it's needed. The fix is really about reporting the targeted indices correctly so that the tasks and other expert APIs don't expose it wrongly.

issue_context.title: EQL sequence queries open PIT against indices not included in search request
comments:
@marshallmain The observation you made regarding PIT and its broad list of targeted indices is something that recently also caught the attention of the Search team, following a series of other related issues: https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/99740
Even though the main observable issue in there is a significantly increased PIT ID size this will consequently have an impact on CPU usage (by simply creating and storing in memory the ID) and on data transfer rates (the bigger the ID the larger the transfer amount).

Irrespective of the information I provided above, this report shouldn't be regarded as a bug since the [EQL usage of the PIT API is correct](https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/8.9/point-in-time-api.html). Relevant extract from the previous docs link:

> A search request with the pit parameter must not specify index, routing, or preference as these parameters are copied from the point in time.

However, I am keeping this issue open as a placeholder for a future improvement to EQL usage of PIT in line with Elasticsearch's work around https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/99740 (ie making sure that any filter passed to an EQL `sequence` or `samples` query will also be copied in the opening PIT request).

Heads up: it is now possible to provide an index_filter as part of the open point in time API, to restrict the indices that a pit will be opened against. All indices that cannot possibly match the filter will be filtered out.
@astefan @siposea Can we please have an update on this issue?
@MikePaquette there is no immediate concrete plan for integrating this, but it is on my radar.

I dug into this issue more today and found a key difference in EQL's usage of Point-in-time compared to the REST `_search` API. When Elasticsearch [parses a search request](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/8.12/server/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/rest/action/search/RestSearchAction.java#L223) that includes a PIT id, it calls `preparePointInTime`. This function verifies that the incoming request does not have indices specified, but [at the end](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/8.12/server/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/rest/action/search/RestSearchAction.java#L413) it extracts the actual index names from the provided PIT id and injects them into the `SearchRequest`. The result is a `SearchRequest` object that **does** specify indices to search against. The final `SearchRequest` with indices can then be passed to the internal `Client` and the request is limited to the correct indices.

The [PITAwareQueryClient](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/8.12/x-pack/plugin/eql/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/eql/execution/search/PITAwareQueryClient.java#L107) in the EQL implementation also builds a `SearchRequest` object, but explicitly sets the indices on the `SearchRequest` object to be empty, whereas in the REST API the indices are extracted from the PIT. Since the final `SearchRequest` built by `PITAwareQueryClient` specifies no indices, when it gets passed to the internal `Client` the query ends up being sent to all indices.

The public facing Elasticsearch docs would apply if EQL used a PIT with the REST API, but since the logic in the REST API that extracts the indices from the PIT id is bypassed when a `SearchRequest` is sent directly to the internal client I don't think the public docs apply here.

As a test I was able to delete the [lines in `PITAwareQueryClient` ](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/8.12/x-pack/plugin/eql/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/eql/execution/search/PITAwareQueryClient.java#L105-L110) that remove the indices from the `SearchRequest`. This way the `SearchRequest` still contains the same indices that were used to open the PIT. After that change the search task created by following the repro steps for this issue had only the single expected index.

That's an excellent observation, thanks @marshallmain. However, the problem description may be a bit misleading. The current issue revolves around the security layer intercepting the search request. In cases where the indices are empty, the security layer expands the indices request as if all (*) were explicitly requested even when a PIT ID is defined on the request. It's crucial to note that this behavior is specific to the security layer.

When the search action receives the request, it disregards the indices set and utilizes only the point in time ID to resolve the indices for the query. Consequently, the request is not broadcasted to all nodes; instead, it is directed only to the shards present in the PIT ID.

The primary challenge lies in the security layer, which performs unnecessary work to determine all the indices accessible to the user making the request. I am actively working on a pull request (PR) to address this issue and will keep you updated on the progress.

review_comments: I guess we should also override setPreference to make sure it throws if point in time is already set, otherwise we rely on order in which the methods are called?

I am just checking the default preference here since it is set by the `RandomizingClient` ctr. If a test using this client sets the preference explicitly an error will be thrown during the execution indicating to the author of the test that preference shouldn't be used in this context.
